claims.text: Introducing a small amount of low-melting, flux-forming dopant into a ceramic powder mixture will lower the required sintering temperature.
The dopant lowers the required sintering temperature by promoting liquid-phase formation.
Liquid-phase formation significantly enhances particle rearrangement at lower temperatures.
Liquid-phase formation significantly enhances diffusion at lower temperatures.
An effective dopant loading is 1–5 wt%.
Mechanical mixing can incorporate the low-melting dopant or flux into the primary ceramic powder.
The proposed doped ceramic can be sintered in air at 200–300 °C below its normal sintering temperature.
Transient liquid phases form during early sintering.
Transient liquid phases enhance mass transport along particle boundaries.
The dopant forms a liquid phase when heated.
The dopant-derived liquid phase wets particle surfaces.
Wetting by the liquid phase reduces diffusion barriers.
Reduced diffusion barriers enable densification at lower temperatures than in undoped powders.
The doped powder will densify at a temperature at least 200 °C lower than conventional sintering.
Lower-temperature sintering of the doped powder will produce density equivalent to or greater than that of the undoped baseline.
Lower-temperature sintering of the doped powder will produce microstructural properties equivalent to or better than those of the undoped baseline.
The undoped ceramic powder requires higher temperatures to achieve similar densification.
Excess dopant can cause unwanted secondary-phase formation.
Excess or poorly selected dopant can degrade mechanical or functional properties.
The achievable temperature reduction and resulting properties depend on dopant chemistry, mixing uniformity, and sintering-cycle parameters.
